question: TalkBack says only "button" on your Compose IconButton and calls the old screen's ImageButton unlabelled — what is missing, and what is the smallest fix for each?
answer:
Neither icon carries a label, and each needs exactly one string: a real `contentDescription` on the `Icon`, and `android:contentDescription` on the `ImageButton`.

### Compose
- The description goes on the `Icon`, not on the `IconButton`. `Modifier.clickable` merges its descendants into one semantics node, so the icon's `contentDescription` becomes the button's label and TalkBack says "Share, button".
- `contentDescription = null` is not a placeholder — it means "this draws nothing a user needs to hear". Null inside a clickable that has no other text leaves a node with a role and no label, which is the bare "button" you are hearing.

### Views
- `android:contentDescription="@string/share"` on the `ImageButton`. Without it TalkBack announces the control as unlabelled and falls back to guessing from the resource id; lint's `ContentDescription` check flags exactly this.
- It has to be a string resource. A literal in the layout ships to every locale in English and never reaches a translator.

The trap is describing the picture instead of the action. "Three dots", "share icon" and "img_share" are all things the user cannot act on; "Share" and "More options" are. And never put "button" or "image" in the description — the role is announced separately, so you get "Share button, button".

Rule of thumb: say the label out loud with the role tacked on the end. "Share, button" is a working screen; "Share icon, button" is the sound of one nobody ever listened to.

question: TalkBack stops on a purely decorative header image, and your unread-count row gets read out twice. Which knob takes each of those out of the node tree?
answer:
`contentDescription = null` and `importantForAccessibility` are different tools — one says there is nothing to announce, the other removes nodes from the tree — and the double reading is neither: it is a grouping problem.

### Taking something out
- Compose: `Image(painter, contentDescription = null)` emits no description property at all, so no node is exposed and TalkBack walks straight past it. That is the intended marker for decoration, not a way to silence a warning.
- `Modifier.clearAndSetSemantics { }` wipes a whole subtree's semantics and replaces them with whatever you set inside — the Compose equivalent of `noHideDescendants`.
- `Modifier.semantics { hideFromAccessibility() }` — the rename of the old experimental `invisibleToUser()` — hides one node from assistive technologies while keeping its semantics for tests.
- Views: `importantForAccessibility="no"` drops the view but keeps its children; `"noHideDescendants"` drops the view and everything under it; `"yes"` forces in a view the framework would skip; `auto`, the default, exposes anything with text, a description or a click listener.

### The double reading
A `contentDescription` on a container does not hide the container's children. They keep their own nodes, so the content is announced once as the group and again item by item. Make the group a single stop: `android:screenReaderFocusable="true"` on the container plus `importantForAccessibility="no"` on each child, or in Compose `Modifier.semantics(mergeDescendants = true) { }`.

Rule of thumb: null and `no` mean "there is nothing here to say". A description means "there is exactly one thing here, and this is it".

question: A rating row reads as five separate stars, and a switch says "on" where the copy should say "Subscribed" — which semantics modifiers fix each of those?
answer:
Merging collapses the five stars into one node, and `stateDescription` renames the spoken state without touching the label.

### Merging and clearing
- `Modifier.semantics(mergeDescendants = true) { }` collapses a subtree into one focus stop and concatenates the children's text. `Modifier.clickable` already does this, which is why a card is one stop and not six.
- Merging stops at a child that merges on its own. A card with an inline "Follow" button stays two nodes, and that is correct — the user has to be able to reach the button.
- A `contentDescription` set on a merging node is appended to the children's text, not substituted for it. `Modifier.clearAndSetSemantics { }` is the tool that replaces a subtree outright, for a chart or a custom gauge whose internals are noise.
- Both trees exist at once: services read the merged tree, and a test can ask for the unmerged one with `useUnmergedTree = true`.

### Describing one control
- `role = Role.Button`, `Role.Checkbox`, `Role.Switch`, `Role.Tab` tell the service what kind of thing it is; `heading()` puts a text node on TalkBack's headings rotor.
- `stateDescription` overrides the spoken state — "Subscribed" instead of "on" — and leaves the label alone, so TalkBack re-reads only the part that changed.
- `onClick(label = "open article")` renames the default action, so TalkBack offers "double tap to open article" instead of "double tap to activate".

Rule of thumb: `contentDescription` is what it is, `stateDescription` is what it is doing right now, `role` is what kind of thing it is, and merging decides how many stops the user makes walking past it.

question: TalkBack says "in list, item 3 of 40" on a RecyclerView row but reads your canvas-drawn chart as one blob — where do those nodes actually come from?
answer:
Nothing is a node until an accessibility service asks: the framework builds `AccessibilityNodeInfo` objects on demand from the View tree, and anything you painted rather than laid out has no node unless you make one.

- Every View contributes one node through `onInitializeAccessibilityNodeInfo`, which you override by attaching a delegate with `ViewCompat.setAccessibilityDelegate` rather than by subclassing the View.
- RecyclerView installs its own delegate. The list node carries `CollectionInfo` (row and column counts) and each bound row carries `CollectionItemInfo` with its index — that is the entire source of "in list, item 3 of 40". Only bound rows exist as nodes, and the total comes from the adapter, so it jumps when you append a page.
- A custom View that paints ten hit areas onto one canvas is one node, because the framework has no idea the canvas has parts. `ExploreByTouchHelper` from `androidx.customview` gives you a virtual node tree: `getVisibleVirtualViews`, `onPopulateNodeForVirtualView`, `onPerformActionForVirtualView`.
- A whole Compose screen is a single `AndroidComposeView`. Its accessibility delegate walks the merged semantics tree and synthesises one virtual node per semantics node — in Compose, semantics IS the node tree, and there is no View per composable.

The trap is tooling that walks Views: to it, a Compose screen is one leaf. That is why Compose tests assert on semantics rather than on view matchers, and why an Espresso accessibility check stops at the `ComposeView` instead of descending into it.

Rule of thumb: if it is not a View and not a semantics node, no assistive technology can see it, however clearly it is drawn.

question: Your list rows delete on swipe and reorder on long-press drag, and a TalkBack user can do neither. What do you add so both operations become reachable?
answer:
Custom accessibility actions: every gesture-only affordance needs a named action on the node, which TalkBack then offers from its actions menu.

### Adding them
- Views: `ViewCompat.addAccessibilityAction(row, getString(R.string.delete)) { _, _ -> delete(id); true }`. It returns an id you can pass to `ViewCompat.removeAccessibilityAction` when the row is rebound.
- `ViewCompat.replaceAccessibilityAction(view, ACTION_CLICK, label, command)` renames the default action rather than adding a second one, so TalkBack says "double tap to open article".
- Compose: `Modifier.semantics { customActions = listOf(CustomAccessibilityAction(label) { onDelete(); true }) }`.
- For reordering, do not try to expose a drag. Expose "Move up" and "Move down" — a drag is impossible for TalkBack and for Switch Access alike, and two extra actions cost nothing.

### Prefer the standard actions
`expand`/`collapse`, `dismiss`, `ACTION_SCROLL_FORWARD` and `ACTION_LONG_CLICK` are localised by the system and understood by every service, including ones you have never heard of. A custom action is only the label you typed, in the language you typed it — so it comes from `strings.xml` like any other user-facing string.

Two traps. The action has to sit on the node the user actually focuses: put it on an inner element of a merged row and it never appears in the menu. And that menu is read aloud one item at a time, so past roughly five actions it stops being usable.

Rule of thumb: anything reachable only by a swipe, a drag, a long press or a pinch does not exist. Give it a name and hang it on the node.

question: An upload finishes and a snackbar slides in. How does a TalkBack user hear about it without losing their place, and why is announceForAccessibility the wrong tool now?
answer:
A live region: the node speaks when its own text changes and accessibility focus never moves — which is exactly why Android 16 deprecated `announceForAccessibility` and the raw `TYPE_ANNOUNCEMENT` event.

### Live regions
- Views: `ViewCompat.setAccessibilityLiveRegion(view, ACCESSIBILITY_LIVE_REGION_POLITE)`. Polite queues behind whatever is being read; assertive interrupts it, and is only for something the user must act on now.
- Compose: `Modifier.semantics { liveRegion = LiveRegionMode.Polite }` on the composable whose text changes. Material's `Snackbar` already does this for you; a toast-like `Box` you drew yourself does not.
- The region speaks on a *change*, so the node has to stay in the tree and take new text. Removing it and adding a different one is a different event, and often says nothing at all.

### Why the announcement API went away
`announceForAccessibility` interrupts, cannot be replayed, leaves nothing on screen to navigate back to, and behaves differently across assistive technologies. The documented replacements are live regions and, for validation, the error channel: `setError` on a `TextView` or on an `AccessibilityNodeInfo` with `CONTENT_CHANGE_TYPE_ERROR`, and `Modifier.semantics { error("Enter a valid email") }` in Compose — which ties the message to the field instead of shouting it into the room.

The trap is a live region on a value that changes every frame: a progress percentage turns polite into a machine gun. Announce in coarse steps, or leave the number on the node and let the user re-read it on demand.

Rule of thumb: prefer changing something the user can navigate back to over speaking at them.

question: A filter sheet opens over the list, TalkBack keeps swiping into the list behind it, and on close the focus jumps to the top of the screen. What do you fix?
answer:
Two independent bugs: the sheet is not modal as far as the node tree is concerned, and nothing hands focus back to the control that opened it.

### Making the sheet the only thing on screen
- `ModalBottomSheet` and `Dialog` render in their own window, so the framework excludes the content behind them and TalkBack treats the sheet as a new pane. A sheet you built as a `Box` on top of the screen has neither property.
- If you did build it yourself: `Modifier.semantics { paneTitle = "Filters" }` on the sheet — in Views, `ViewCompat.setAccessibilityPaneTitle` — makes TalkBack announce it when it appears, and `Modifier.clearAndSetSemantics { }` on the content behind it (`importantForAccessibility="noHideDescendants"` in Views) is what actually stops the swipe from walking into the list.
- Material's own sheets announce a pane title rather than seizing focus, and that is the behaviour to copy: announce, do not grab.

### Order, and getting focus back
- Default order is the hierarchy in Views and a geometry-based sort in Compose. When that disagrees with the visual layout, use `android:accessibilityTraversalBefore`/`After`, or in Compose `isTraversalGroup = true` on the container plus `traversalIndex` on its children — `isTraversalGroup` replaced the deprecated `isContainer` flag in Compose 1.5.
- On close, put focus back where it came from: keep a `FocusRequester` on the button that opened the sheet and call `requestFocus()`, or in Views `performAccessibilityAction(ACTION_ACCESSIBILITY_FOCUS, null)` on that view.

The trap is that `traversalIndex` only orders elements inside the same traversal group, and a traversal hint pointing across containers or forming a cycle is ignored. Reordering is a last resort; laying the thing out in the order it should be read is the fix that keeps working.

Rule of thumb: a modal is a place, not a layer. If the user can swipe out of it, it is not modal.

question: Your 24dp icon buttons sit 4dp apart and the brand blue on white measures 3.4:1. Which numbers must you actually hit, and how, without redrawing anything?
answer:
48x48dp of touch target per control with 8dp between them, and 4.5:1 for body text — and both can be met without changing a single drawn pixel.

### Touch targets
- The icon stays 24dp; the target around it grows to 48dp. Material 3 in Compose already does this for its own controls: `IconButton`, `Checkbox`, `RadioButton` and `Switch` apply `Modifier.minimumInteractiveComponentSize()`, which reserves the space without resizing the visual.
- `LocalMinimumInteractiveComponentSize` is the knob — it replaced the deprecated boolean `LocalMinimumInteractiveComponentEnforcement` — and providing `Dp.Unspecified` switches enforcement off, which should be a decision rather than an accident.
- In your own composable the modifier order decides everything. `Modifier.size(24.dp).clickable { }` is a 24dp target; `Modifier.clickable { }.padding(12.dp).size(24.dp)` is 48dp. Padding declared after `clickable` sits inside the target.
- In Views: 48dp `minWidth`/`minHeight`, or a `TouchDelegate` — with the caveat that a touch delegate grows only the touch area, not the node bounds a service reads or the rectangle TalkBack draws around the focused element.

### Contrast
- 4.5:1 for text below 24sp (18.7sp bold), 3:1 above it, and 3:1 for icons, input borders and focus indicators.
- Hint and placeholder text is text and has to pass; that grey at 2.8:1 is the usual failure. Disabled controls are exempt, which is not an invitation to disable more of them.
- Text over a photo or a gradient has no single ratio. Put a scrim underneath and measure against the worst pixel that can end up behind it.

Rule of thumb: contrast is measured against what is actually behind the pixel, and a touch target is measured against a fingertip, not against the icon.

question: At 200% font size a fixed 56dp row clips its label while the price beside it does not grow at all — what did that layout get wrong?
answer:
Text sized in `dp` opts out of the user's font preference entirely, and a container with a fixed `dp` height has nowhere to put the text that does scale.

### What sp actually does now
- `sp` is `dp` multiplied by the user's font scale; `dp` is fixed. `android:textSize="16dp"` and a Compose `fontSize` built out of a `Dp` both ignore the setting — lint's `SpUsage` catches the XML case, nothing catches the Compose one.
- Android 14 (API 34) raised the ceiling to 200% and made the curve non-linear: small text grows almost in full, an already-large headline grows much less. A 12sp caption and a 32sp title no longer scale by the same factor.
- That is why `sp * fontScale * density` is now wrong. Convert with `TypedValue.applyDimension(COMPLEX_UNIT_SP, …)` and back with `TypedValue.deriveDimension(…)` (API 34+); in Compose `with(LocalDensity.current) { 16.sp.toDp() }` already applies the right curve.

### What breaks first
- Fixed heights — `layout_height="56dp"`, `Modifier.height(56.dp)` — and any `minHeight` someone quietly turned into a real height. Use `wrap_content` or `Modifier.heightIn(min = 56.dp)`.
- `maxLines = 1` with ellipsis on a label the user must read: the words vanish instead of wrapping.
- Two texts side by side in a rigid `Row` — give one `weight(1f)`, or stack them past a threshold with `FlowRow`.

Rule of thumb: `sp` for anything with words in it, `dp` for everything you draw, and no fixed height on a box that contains text. Check it with `@Preview(fontScale = 2f)` and `adb shell settings put system font_scale 2.0` before QA does.

question: Your screen passes Accessibility Scanner and the Espresso accessibility checks, and a blind tester still cannot finish checkout — what do those tools not check?
answer:
Automated checks prove that a label, a touch target or a contrast ratio exists; only a person driving TalkBack can tell you whether the label means anything and whether the task can be completed.

### What the automation covers
- Accessibility Scanner (a Play Store app, run on device) audits one screen at a time: missing item labels, duplicated labels, touch targets under 48dp, text contrast, clickable items nested inside clickable items.
- Espresso: `AccessibilityChecks.enable().setRunChecksFromRootView(true)` from `androidx.test.espresso:espresso-accessibility` runs the same Accessibility Test Framework rules before every view interaction, and `setSuppressingResultMatcher` lets you carry a known failure instead of disabling the lot.
- Compose instrumented tests: `enableAccessibilityChecks()` on the rule runs ATF over the composed hierarchy, and the semantics tree is directly assertable — `assertContentDescriptionEquals`, `assert(hasClickAction())`, `assertHeightIsAtLeast(48.dp)`.
- Cheaper still: lint's `ContentDescription` and `ClickableViewAccessibility`, and the Play Console pre-launch report, which runs ATF on real devices.

### What only a human finds
- Labels that exist and say nothing: "image", "button1", an icon's file name.
- A reading order that is legal but senseless, and focus that lands nowhere when a dialog or bottom sheet opens.
- Announcements that never fire, or fire so often they talk over the user.
- Whether a custom action is discoverable at all, and whether the whole flow works with swipe navigation and no precise double-tap.

Mental model: the automated pass is a spell-checker. It proves the words are there, never that the sentence makes sense — so budget one manual TalkBack run per feature, screen curtain on.

question: Your Russian build shows "5 товар" and a banner prints its two arguments in the wrong order — what is missing from strings.xml?
answer:
Both are the same mistake: the sentence was built for English grammar — a hand-picked suffix and a fixed argument order — instead of being handed whole to the resource system so the translation can decide.

### Positional arguments
- With more than one substitution aapt2 requires the positional form `%1$s`, `%2$d`; two bare `%s` is a build error. Even a single `%s` is a trap, because a translator cannot move it once a second argument appears.
- The index is the argument's identity, so a translation is free to write `%2$s` first. A literal percent is `%%`, an apostrophe is `\'`.
- Wrap each placeholder in `<xliff:g id="name" example="Anna">%1$s</xliff:g>` so the translation tool locks it and shows the translator a sample value.

### Plurals
- `<plurals>` items carry CLDR categories, not numbers: `zero`, `one`, `two`, `few`, `many`, `other`. Which ones exist is a property of the language, never of your string — English uses `one` and `other`; Russian needs `one` (1, 21, 31), `few` (2–4, 22–24), `many` (0, 5–20, 25–30) and `other` for fractions; Arabic uses all six.
- `getQuantityString(R.plurals.cart_count, count, count)` passes `count` twice on purpose: the first selects the category, the second fills `%1$d`. Pass it once and you get a `MissingFormatArgumentException`. In Compose it is `pluralStringResource(R.plurals.cart_count, count, count)`.
- `<item quantity="zero">` in an English file is dead code — English has no `zero` category, so 0 takes `other`. A real empty-state line is a separate string chosen in code.
- Never assemble a sentence from fragments: another language may inflect the noun around the number or put the number somewhere else entirely.

Rule: if a count, a name or a date goes into a sentence, the whole sentence lives in `strings.xml` with positional placeholders, and anything counted is a plural. Lint's `ImpliedQuantity` and `StringFormatMatches` catch the ones you forget.
code_example:
<!-- res/values/strings.xml -->
<resources xmlns:xliff="urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:1.2">

  <!-- WRONG: two non-positional args (a build error), and a noun glued to a number
  <string name="moved">Moved %s to %s</string>
  <string name="cart_count">items in cart</string>
  -->

  <!-- Shown after a file is moved. %1$s is the file, %2$s the folder. -->
  <string name="moved">
    Moved <xliff:g id="file" example="report.pdf">%1$s</xliff:g>
    to <xliff:g id="folder" example="Archive">%2$s</xliff:g>
  </string>

  <plurals name="cart_count">
    <item quantity="one"><xliff:g id="count">%1$d</xliff:g> item in cart</item>
    <item quantity="other"><xliff:g id="count">%1$d</xliff:g> items in cart</item>
  </plurals>

  <!-- The empty state is its own string, not quantity="zero" -->
  <string name="cart_empty">Your cart is empty</string>

  <string name="event_checkout" translatable="false">checkout_paid</string>
</resources>

<!-- res/values-ru/strings.xml — the translator adds the categories Russian needs
  <plurals name="cart_count">
    <item quantity="one">%1$d товар в корзине</item>
    <item quantity="few">%1$d товара в корзине</item>
    <item quantity="many">%1$d товаров в корзине</item>
    <item quantity="other">%1$d товара в корзине</item>
  </plurals>
-->

<!-- Call sites: the count is passed twice — it selects, then it fills
  getString(R.string.moved, file.name, folder.name)
  resources.getQuantityString(R.plurals.cart_count, count, count)
  pluralStringResource(R.plurals.cart_count, count, count)
-->

question: Your app ships English in values/ and a values-ru; a user whose language list is Ukrainian then Russian opens it and gets Russian — is that a bug?
answer:
No — since API 24 the user has an ordered `LocaleList`, and Android walks all of it before it ever falls back to the unqualified `values/`, so their second choice beats your default.

### How the match runs
- For each entry in the list the system tries an exact qualifier match, then that locale's parent chain: `en-GB` → `en-001` → `en`, `es-MX` → `es-419` → `es`. Ukrainian matches nothing here, Russian matches `values-ru`, and the search stops there.
- A near miss also counts now: a `fr-CH` user finds `values-fr-rFR` instead of dropping to the default, which is what API 23 did and what surprised everyone.
- That is why region-qualifying your source language is a bug waiting to happen. English belongs in `values/`; `values-en-rGB` is only for the words that genuinely differ (colour, postcode). Scripts use the BCP-47 form: `values-b+sr+Latn`, `values-b+zh+Hans`.
- `values/` must define every string. `MissingDefaultResource` in lint and a crash at lookup are the two ways you learn it did not.

### Trimming, and reading it back
- `androidResources.localeFilters` (AGP 8.10+; previously locale entries in `resourceConfigurations`/`resConfigs`) keeps only the locales you list, and it strips them out of AppCompat and Play Services too. A user whose language you filtered out silently gets the default.
- Read the effective locale from the configuration — `resources.configuration.locales[0]`, or `LocalConfiguration.current.locales[0]` in Compose — never from a `Locale` captured once at process start, because a per-app language change or a configuration change moves it under you.

Rule of thumb: the unqualified folder is your source language, every other language gets a plain language qualifier, and a region qualifier only when the region really changes the words.

question: A user picks Russian in your in-app language switcher, but after a cold start the app is English again and their push notifications never switched — what is missing?
answer:
Nothing persists an app locale unless you go through the per-app language API — `AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales()` on top of a declared `locales_config.xml` — and the server that composes your push text has never heard of that choice at all.

### Wiring it up
- `res/xml/locales_config.xml` lists the locales you ship, and `android:localeConfig="@xml/locales_config"` on `<application>` points at it. AGP can write the file for you with `androidResources.generateLocaleConfig = true`. Declaring it is also what puts your app under Settings → System → Languages → App languages on Android 13+.
- `AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales(LocaleListCompat.forLanguageTags("ru"))` is one call for every API level. On 33+ it delegates to the framework `LocaleManager`, which stores the choice system-side and recreates your activities; below 33 AppCompat stores it itself, which needs the `autoStoreLocales` meta-data on `AppLocalesMetadataHolderService` enabled.
- Read it back with `AppCompatDelegate.getApplicationLocales()`. An empty list means "follow the system" — that is the state your switcher needs for its default row, and it is not the same as the current system language.

### The two things that still break
- App Bundle language splits: the device only installs the languages it asked for, so switching to one it never had shows your default strings. Request it first with `SplitInstallManager.startInstall(… addLanguage(locale) …)`, or turn the split off with `bundle { language { enableSplit = false } }`.
- Anything your app does not draw: push text composed on the server, the store listing, `android:label`. Send the app locale to the backend whenever it changes.

Rule of thumb: `locales_config.xml` is the contract, `setApplicationLocales` is the only writer, and everything rendered outside your process has to be told separately.

question: The Arabic build mirrors everywhere except a progress bar you drew with Canvas and a chevron still pointing right — what does Android mirror for you, and what never will?
answer:
With `android:supportsRtl="true"` the framework mirrors layout attributes and auto-mirrored drawables, and that is the whole list — anything you positioned absolutely, drew yourself, or shipped as a plain directional asset keeps pointing the way you drew it.

### What mirrors on its own
- Layout: `paddingStart`/`paddingEnd`, `layout_marginStart`/`End`, `gravity="start"`, `drawableStart`, ConstraintLayout's `layout_constraintStart_toStartOf`. In Compose `Modifier.padding(start = …)`, `Arrangement.Start`, `Modifier.offset` and `placeRelative` are all direction-aware; `absolutePadding`, `Alignment.Absolute.*`, `absoluteOffset` and `place` deliberately are not.
- Drawables with `android:autoMirrored="true"` — vectors and nine-patches. In Compose use `Icons.AutoMirrored.Filled.ArrowBack`; the old `Icons.Filled.ArrowBack` is deprecated for exactly this reason.

### What never does
- Canvas and custom layout: read `LocalLayoutDirection.current` (or `View.getLayoutDirection()`) and mirror the coordinates yourself. Your chevron needs `autoMirrored` on the asset, or a `graphicsLayer { scaleX = -1f }` when it is drawn.
- Icons that are not about reading order: media transport controls, a logo, a checkmark, a picture of a physical object. Mirroring play and fast-forward is the classic overcorrection — a timeline runs the same way in every language.
- Bidirectional runs inside a sentence: an order number, a phone number, a URL or a Latin brand name dropped into Arabic text drags its punctuation to the wrong end. Wrap the value with `BidiFormatter.getInstance().unicodeWrap(value)`, which inserts the isolate characters so the run keeps its own direction.

Test it before a single Arabic string exists: build with `isPseudoLocalesEnabled` and run in `ar-XB`, or flip Developer options → Force RTL (`adb shell settings put global debug.force_rtl 1`).

question: A Thai user's receipt shows the year 2569, an Egyptian user's amount fails to parse, and a German sees $1,234.50 on a euro price — what do those three share?
answer:
All three are strings the app assembled itself instead of asking a locale-aware formatter: a pattern with the default locale, a number parsed with `toDouble()`, and a currency symbol pasted next to `String.format`.

### Dates and times
- Display formats come from `DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedDate(FormatStyle.MEDIUM).withLocale(locale).withZone(zone)`, or from `DateFormat.getBestDateTimePattern(locale, "MMMd")` when you need one specific set of fields. A pattern you typed yourself is only ever for machine-readable output.
- `SimpleDateFormat("dd/MM/yyyy")` with no locale follows the user's: Arabic locales render the digits as ٢٠٢٦ and a Thai device can hand you a Buddhist year. If you must have a stable format, pass `Locale.ROOT` explicitly.
- Store an `Instant` or epoch millis and convert at the edge with `ZoneId.systemDefault()`, re-read per render — the device's zone changes mid-session on a flight. Below API 26 `java.time` needs core library desugaring.

### Numbers, currency and lists
- `NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(locale)` decides the separators and where the symbol goes; `Currency.getInstance("EUR")` decides what the money is. The locale must never pick the currency — a German looking at a dollar price still owes dollars.
- Parse with `NumberFormat.parse`, never `String.toDouble()`: `1.234,50` and `١٢٣٤` are both legal user input, and both throw.
- `android.icu.text` covers the rest — `RelativeDateTimeFormatter` for "3 days ago", `ListFormatter` for "a, b and c", `MeasureFormat` for units, and `MessageFormat` when a `<plurals>` cannot express the sentence.

Rule of thumb: no `+` and no separator you typed ever touches a number or a date a person will read. If you wrote a pattern string for human output, it is probably a bug in a language you do not speak.
code_example:
// WRONG — three bugs in three lines
val date = SimpleDateFormat("dd/MM/yyyy").format(order.date)  // follows the user's locale
val total = "$" + String.format("%.2f", order.amount)         // always dollars
val parsed = input.toDouble()                                 // throws on "1.234,50"

// RIGHT — the locale formats; the data decides what is being formatted
private fun locale(res: Resources): Locale = res.configuration.locales[0]

fun formatDate(instant: Instant, res: Resources): String =
  DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedDate(FormatStyle.MEDIUM)
    .withLocale(locale(res))
    .withZone(ZoneId.systemDefault())        // read per render, never cached
    .format(instant)

fun formatMoney(minorUnits: Long, code: String, res: Resources): String =
  NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(locale(res)).apply {
    currency = Currency.getInstance(code)    // EUR stays EUR on an en-US phone
    minimumFractionDigits = currency.defaultFractionDigits
  }.format(minorUnits / 100.0)

fun parseAmount(text: String, res: Resources): Double =
  NumberFormat.getInstance(locale(res)).parse(text)?.toDouble()
    ?: throw NumberFormatException(text)

// Machine-readable output pins the locale instead of following the user
val fileName = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd", Locale.ROOT)
  .withZone(ZoneOffset.UTC)
  .format(Instant.now())

// ICU owns the rest of the sentence too
val ago = RelativeDateTimeFormatter.getInstance(ULocale.forLocale(locale(res)))
  .format(3.0, Direction.LAST, RelativeUnit.DAYS)          // "3 days ago"
val authors = ListFormatter.getInstance(locale(res))
  .format(listOf("Anna", "Bo", "Cy"))                      // "Anna, Bo, and Cy"

question: Translations for twenty locales will land three days before the release branch cuts — what do you put in place now so that week is boring?
answer:
Everything except the translations themselves can be done before they arrive: pseudolocales prove the layouts survive, lint proves nothing is hard-coded, and a string freeze decides what the translators are actually given.

### Before the strings go out
- Turn on pseudolocales: `buildTypes { debug { isPseudoLocalesEnabled = true } }` adds `en-XA` — accented, about 30% longer, bracketed, so every truncation shows up and every hard-coded string stays conspicuously plain ASCII — and `ar-XB`, which is RTL with reversed text.
- Make lint fail the build on `HardcodedText`, `StringFormatInvalid`, `StringFormatMatches` and `ImpliedQuantity`, and run `lintRelease` in CI with `abortOnError = true`. `MissingTranslation` starts earning its keep the day the first locale lands.
- Give the translator context they cannot get from the string: a `<!-- -->` comment above it, and `<xliff:g id="name" example="Anna">%1$s</xliff:g>` around every placeholder. Mark keys, analytics names and debug text `translatable="false"`.

### The week itself
- Freeze on a date, hand over `values/strings.xml`, and accept that anything added afterwards ships in your default language — the fallback is silent, so keep the list of what missed the cut.
- Screenshot the main screens in `en-XA` and `ar-XB` in CI (Paparazzi or Roborazzi, or `@Preview(locale = "en-XA")`) so a truncation is a failing diff rather than a bug report from Berlin.
- Remember what is not in `strings.xml` at all: `android:label`, the Play listing, server-composed push text, and anything a widget or Wear surface draws.

Rule of thumb: a locale you cannot test before its translation exists is a locale you will ship broken. `en-XA` is the whole trick.
